section.title: Justice and the Sovereign LORD
section.sectionRationale: Closing out much of the first Solomonic collection, 10:1 to 22:16, this chapter opens with the king's heart as a waterway in the LORD's hand and returns repeatedly to His sovereignty over plans, sacrifices, and even the outcome of battle, while pressing hard on justice, righteousness, and the futility of wickedness.
section.thesis: The LORD directs even the king's heart and weighs every heart's true motives, so that no scheme, sacrifice, or army can prevail against Him, and His people are called to righteousness and justice rather than the crooked shortcuts that ultimately sweep the wicked away.
section.frameNote: Five clusters: the king's heart in the LORD's hand and righteousness over sacrifice; the crooked way and its cost; justice as joy to the righteous and terror to evildoers; the quarrelsome home and the wisdom that outlasts strongholds; final counsel on speech, pride, and the LORD's victory over every plan.

units.label: The king's heart in the LORD's hand

verses.text: The king's heart is a waterway in the hand of the LORD; He directs it where He pleases.
All a man's ways seem right to him, but the LORD weighs the heart.
To do righteousness and justice is more desirable to the LORD than sacrifice.
Haughty eyes and a proud heart, the guides of the wicked, are sin.

units.label: The crooked way and its cost

verses.text: The plans of the diligent bring plenty, as surely as haste leads to poverty.
Making a fortune by a lying tongue is a vanishing mist, a deadly pursuit.
The violence of the wicked will sweep them away because they refuse to do what is just.
The way of a guilty man is crooked, but the conduct of the innocent is upright.
Better to live on a corner of the roof than to share a house with a quarrelsome wife.

units.label: Justice as joy or terror
units.note: the wicked man's soul craves evil

verses.text: The soul of the wicked man craves evil; his neighbor finds no favor in his eyes.
When a mocker is punished, the simple gain wisdom; and when a wise man is instructed, he acquires knowledge.
The Righteous One considers the house of the wicked and brings the wicked to ruin.
Whoever shuts his ears to the cry of the poor, he too shall cry out and receive no answer.
A gift in secret soothes anger, and a covert bribe pacifies great wrath.
{{mishpat|Justice}} executed is a joy to the righteous, but a terror to the workers of iniquity.

units.label: The quarrelsome home and lasting wisdom
units.note: wisdom scales the city of the mighty

verses.text: The man who strays from the path of understanding will rest in the assembly of the dead.
He who loves pleasure will become poor; the one who loves wine and oil will never be rich.
The wicked become a ransom for the righteous, and the faithless for the upright.
Better to live in the desert than with a contentious and ill-tempered wife.
Precious treasures and oil are in the dwelling of the wise, but a foolish man consumes them.
He who pursues righteousness and loving devotion finds life, righteousness, and honor.
A wise man scales the city of the mighty and pulls down the stronghold in which they trust.

units.label: Final counsel: speech, pride, and the LORD's victory
units.note: no wisdom can prevail against the LORD

verses.text: He who guards his mouth and tongue keeps his soul from distress.
Mocker is the name of the proud and arrogant man, of him who acts with excessive pride.
The craving of the slacker kills him because his hands refuse to work.
All day long he covets more, but the righteous give without restraint.
The sacrifice of the wicked is detestable, how much more so when brought with ill intent!
A lying witness will perish, but the man who listens to truth will speak forever.
A wicked man hardens his face, but the upright man makes his way sure.
There is no wisdom, no understanding, no counsel that can prevail against the LORD.
A horse is prepared for the day of battle, but victory is of the LORD.

mishpat.gloss: Justice, judgment, the right verdict or order of things. Verse 15 says justice executed brings joy to the righteous but terror to evildoers, the same word used throughout Scripture for God's own righteous rule, which His people are to reflect in their courts and dealings.

basic.context: This chapter opens with a striking claim: even the king's heart, the most powerful will in the land, is like a stream the LORD directs wherever He pleases. From there it moves through warnings against pride, crookedness, and violence, insisting that righteousness and justice matter to God more than religious ritual, and it ends by declaring that no human wisdom or army can prevail against the LORD.
basic.hermeneutics: These proverbs describe how life under God's sovereignty generally works, they are not mechanical guarantees for every individual case. The chapter's repeated refrain, that the LORD directs kings, weighs hearts, and gives victory, teaches a theology of providence that undergirds practical wisdom about justice, honesty, and humility.
basic.originalLanguages: Mishpat, justice, verse 15, names the right ordering of relationships and courts that God both requires and enacts; when justice is executed it brings joy to the righteous and terror to evildoers, showing that justice is never neutral, it always lands somewhere. The chapter's vision of the LORD directing the king's heart 'like a waterway,' verse 1, uses an irrigation image familiar to ancient farmers who channeled water exactly where they willed.
basic.typology: The king's heart directed like a waterway in the LORD's hand, verse 1, anticipates the greater truth that all authority, even hostile authority, ultimately serves God's purposes, as seen when Pilate's power over Jesus was itself given from above, John 19:11. The declaration that no wisdom can prevail against the LORD, verse 30, points to the final defeat of every power raised against Christ.
basic.christ: Verse 1's picture of even a king's heart directed by the LORD anticipates Jesus' words to Pilate, that his authority over Him was given from above, John 19:11, showing that the cross itself unfolded under the same sovereign hand that directs kings. Verse 3's preference for righteousness and justice over sacrifice foreshadows Christ, who both perfectly enacted justice and became the once for all sacrifice that religious ritual alone could never supply.
basic.god: God directs even the most powerful human hearts like water in a channel, verse 1, and weighs every heart's true motives rather than its self-justifying appearance, verse 2. He values justice and righteousness far above ritual sacrifice, verse 3, and no combination of human wisdom, understanding, or counsel can ever stand against Him, verse 30, so that even victory in battle belongs to Him alone, verse 31.
basic.crossReferences: John 19:11 echoes verse 1's truth that all authority is given from above. 1 Samuel 15:22 echoes verse 3's preference for obedience and justice over sacrifice. Isaiah 40:23-24 echoes the futility of counsel against the LORD in verse 30. Psalm 20:7 echoes verse 31, trusting not in horses but in the name of the LORD.
basic.oneStory: Proverbs 21 declares that the LORD sovereignly directs even the mightiest human hearts, prizes justice and righteousness above ritual, and gives victory that no human scheme can prevent or secure. The whole Bible's story runs on this same sovereignty, finally displayed at the cross, where the highest human power served God's saving purpose in Christ, the true and better sacrifice.

context.literary:
Proverbs 21 is bracketed by the LORD's hand. Verse 1 puts the king's heart in it, 'in the hand of the LORD', and verse 31 gives the last word to Him: victory 'is of the LORD'. Between them the chapter hangs one theme on another with the usual catchword method. Heart and weighing in verse 2 lead to sacrifice in verse 3, pride in verse 4, and plans in verse 5. Verses 9 and 19 are twins about a quarrelsome wife and a lonely roof or desert, and verse 9 is repeated word for word in 25:24. Verses 6 and 7 move from fortune made by a lying tongue to the violence that sweeps the wicked away.

Look for the pairs. Verses 3 and 27 are a pair too, both about the sacrifice of the wicked and God's refusal of it. In verse 11 the simple gain wisdom when a mocker is punished, repeating the logic of 19:25. Near the end, verse 30 says no wisdom or counsel can stand against the LORD, and verse 31 sets even the war horse beneath Him, so that the last two sayings widen the first verse from one king's heart to every human resource.

The writing is mostly antithetic, 'but' joining a pair, and the two lines of verse 1 are an exception. They form a single sentence with a single claim, that the king is a stream and the LORD the hand that turns it. This is the thesis, and the rest of the chapter works it out in miniature: in courts, in homes, in markets and on battlefields.
context.historical:
The chapter was written for hearers who knew what power was. Kings in the Near East commanded armies, taxes and temples, and people believed their decisions could not be countered. To say that the king's heart is in the LORD's hand like a channel was a claim about who is really in charge. Water channels were part of the farmer's world, and the image of a ditch dug and opened to send water where the farmer wills is a domestic one. The Preacher of Ecclesiastes mentions the reservoirs he built to water his groves, Ecclesiastes 2:6. The farmer turns water with a spade, and the LORD turns a king.

The history of Israel supplied the examples. The LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, Exodus 7:3, and Pharaoh also hardened his own, Exodus 8:15. Later, the LORD 'stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia' to send a proclamation to release the exiles, Ezra 1:1, and a pagan king did the LORD's will without knowing His name.

Verse 3's priority of righteousness and justice over sacrifice needs a temple to be heard. Under Solomon there was a great temple and a busy altar, and the temptation was to think that costly worship made up for injustice. The prophets say the same as the proverb, Isaiah 1:11 to 17, Micah 6:6 to 8.

Verse 31 would remind its hearers of the wars of the kings. Solomon himself collected 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horses, 1 Kings 10:26, even though the law said a king must not multiply horses, Deuteronomy 17:16, and the sages knew the temptation to trust the horse. The proverb sets that trust beside the LORD.
context.canonical:
Verse 1 is the theme of the Bible's account of history. Isaiah says the LORD can use Assyria as a rod, and Daniel confesses that God 'does as He pleases with the army of heaven and the peoples of the earth', Daniel 4:35. Paul takes the same truth to the Roman government, 'there is no authority except that which is from God', Romans 13:1, and John to the beast's own kings: 'God has put it into their hearts to carry out His purpose', Revelation 17:17. The proverb is the start of this long line and it makes the claim in one verse.

Verse 3 is the voice of the prophets in embryo. Samuel tells Saul that 'obedience is better than sacrifice', 1 Samuel 15:22. Hosea speaks for God: 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice', Hosea 6:6, and Jesus quotes that verse twice, Matthew 9:13 and 12:7. Micah's summary that the LORD requires 'to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly' answers the same question as the proverb, Micah 6:8. Psalm 51:16 to 17 shows what God wants in place of the offering: a broken and contrite heart.

Verse 2 is repeated in 16:2, and verse 31 is a Proverbs version of Psalm 20:7 and Psalm 33:16 to 17. Verse 13, that whoever shuts his ear to the poor will cry out unheard, stands behind James 2:13, 'judgment without mercy will be shown to anyone who has not been merciful', and behind the parable of the unforgiving servant, Matthew 18:23 to 35.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The sage wants his hearer to hold two things that do not feel natural together. He must act, and he must know he is not in control. The chapter has a great deal of practical wisdom, such as plans that succeed by diligence, a guarded tongue, and generosity, and it has a deep humbling truth beside it: the king's heart, the sacrifice, the battle and the hidden motive all belong to the LORD.

His second aim is a corrective on religion. Verse 3 and verse 27 warn that worship does not buy off injustice. A pupil who is in the habit of thinking that the right ritual puts him right with God is told to look at how he treats the weak and what he intends when he comes to the altar.

His third aim is protection. Verse 30 and 31 are the sage's answer to fear of powerful people and of armies. Those who do justice may be tempted to give up when the other side holds the throne or the horses. The teacher tells them that the opposition has the one disadvantage that cannot be overcome, that it is against the LORD.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Verses 1, 2, 30 and 31 are descriptions of God, not commands. They tell us what is the case, and the other verses tell us how to live in light of it. The mistake to avoid is turning the descriptions into excuses. 'The LORD directs the king' does not mean the king may not be criticised, and 'victory is of the LORD' does not mean a nation need not prepare. The phrase 'a horse is prepared for the day of battle' says that preparation is wise and expected; the point is that it is not the final cause.

Commands are plainer. Verses 3 and 21 point to doing righteousness and justice, 13 calls for an open ear to the cry of the poor, and 23 asks for a guarded mouth. Observations like verse 17 (the pleasure lover grows poor) and verse 25 (the craving of the slacker kills him) show how habits end.

Verse 14 needs special care. A gift in secret soothes anger, and a covert bribe pacifies great wrath: it describes what works, not what is right. Elsewhere the sages condemn bribery plainly, 17:23, and the law forbids it, Exodus 23:8, so the proverb reports a custom the book does not endorse.

Verse 9 and verse 19 are the best known of the chapter, and they report how misery feels, and do not teach that a spouse is the problem. They are included to speak to the person who makes a home hard to live in, and a modern reader should apply them to anyone, of any sex, who makes peace impossible.

debates.question: How can the LORD direct a king's heart and still hold the king responsible?

views.label: God's direction overrules and so the king is a tool
views.case: The image is of a channel dug by a farmer. Water has no say. Texts like Romans 9:17 to 18, 'He hardens whom He wants to harden', are read as God's decisive action leaving the human will no independent role.

views.label: God directs through the king's own willing, and the king answers for what he wills
views.case: The Pharaoh story has both lines: the LORD says He will harden Pharaoh's heart, Exodus 7:3, and Pharaoh also hardens his own, Exodus 8:15. Acts 2:23 says Jesus was delivered by God's set plan and put to death by the hands of the lawless, in the same breath. The same Scripture holds both.

views.label: The verse is about the limit of royal power, not the mechanics of choice
views.case: The aim is to say that no king is beyond the LORD's reach. The text does not offer a theory of free will but a doxology about God's reach.

debates.bearing: The Bible refuses to settle the matter by removing either side. The proverb serves worship and trust: the believer is not afraid of rulers, and the ruler cannot say God made him do it.

debates.question: Who is 'the Righteous One' of verse 12?

views.label: God Himself
views.case: The BSB capitalises it and the footnote offers 'the righteous one' as the alternative. The verse gives the one who 'considers the house of the wicked and brings the wicked to ruin', which is the work of the LORD, verse 12 follows verse 2's picture of one who weighs.

views.label: A righteous person, perhaps the righteous king
views.case: The Hebrew has no capital, and the word is a common description of a person. A righteous man or king can consider the household of a wicked man and act, as the Davidic ideal sketched in Psalm 101:5 to 8.

views.label: Either, and the ambiguity is the point
views.case: A faithful ruler's justice mirrors God's, so the sentence can be read at both levels. The later Christian reading hears in it the Righteous One of Acts 3:14 and sees the verse fulfilled in Him.

debates.bearing: All three readings agree that wickedness is not the final word, because someone righteous is paying attention to the wicked house. The choice affects emphasis, not the doctrine.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 uses a rare agricultural picture. The word for 'waterway' is a plural of peleg, a channel or watercourse, and the verb 'directs' is natah, to stretch out, bend or incline, a verb used of turning or inclining something in a chosen direction. The two lines say the king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, and wherever He delights, chafets, He turns it. The verb of delight is the same used of God's pleasure in Isaiah 46:10, 'all My good pleasure I will accomplish'.

The verb of verse 2, 'weighs', is tochen, found also in 16:2 and 24:12, where it is the LORD who weighs hearts. The sentence sets a person's own estimate, 'right in his eyes', beside the LORD's balance, and the picture of a scale makes the contrast one of accuracy: only one of the two assessments is true.

Verse 4 is a famous crux. The key word in the traditional text is spelled nir, which elsewhere means ploughed ground, and it is very close to ner, a lamp. Translators differ on which is meant. The BSB translates it 'guides'. Whichever sense is right, the verse links haughty eyes and a proud heart with sin, and calls both 'sin'.

Verse 6 describes wealth got by lying as hevel nidaf, a breath that is driven away. Hevel is Ecclesiastes' word, 'vanity', and means a vapour or puff of air. The picture is of a fortune that evaporates under the hand. The following Hebrew is difficult, and the BSB reads 'a deadly pursuit', where others read a seeking of death.

Verse 16 says the wanderer 'will rest in the assembly of the dead'. The word for the dead is repha'im, the shades, found also in 2:18 and 9:18. Rest is an ironic word: the person who strays finds a rest he did not want.

Verse 18 calls the wicked a ransom, kofer. It is from the same root as the verb for covering and atoning, kipper, and Isaiah 43:3 uses it when the LORD says He gives Egypt as a ransom for Israel. Proverbs 11:8 has the same exchange of places between righteous and wicked. Last, in verse 31 the word for victory is teshu'ah, from the root for salvation, so the line reads: the horse is made ready, but deliverance belongs to the LORD.

typology.type: The king whose heart is a channel in the LORD's hand, verse 1
typology.fulfillment: The channel is turned wherever God pleases, and the New Testament shows the pattern at its darkest. Pilate holds the power of life and death, and Jesus tells him, 'You would have no authority over Me if it were not given to you from above', John 19:11. The authorities who killed Jesus 'carried out what Your hand and will had decided beforehand', Acts 4:28. The escalation is that the greatest evil in history becomes the means of salvation. The type falls short as a model for Christ Himself, because He is no mere channel: He lays down His life of His own will, John 10:18.

typology.type: Righteousness and justice above sacrifice, verse 3
typology.fulfillment: Israel's sacrifices pointed toward something they could not do. Obedience and mercy are what the sacrifices were for, as Samuel, Hosea and Micah say. Jesus quotes Hosea, 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice', Matthew 9:13, and then perfectly does both: He enacts justice and mercy in His life and, in His death, offers the sacrifice that no animal could be, Hebrews 10:5 to 10. The type is surpassed because the choice between justice and sacrifice, which the proverb poses, is resolved in a person who is both the righteous One and the offering.

typology.type: The wicked as ransom for the righteous, verse 18
typology.fulfillment: The proverb states a pattern of exchange in which the guilty take the place of the innocent, as Haman hangs on the gallows he built for Mordecai, Esther 7:10. The gospel reverses it. The Righteous One becomes the ransom for the guilty: the Son of Man came 'to give His life as a ransom for many', Mark 10:45, and 'gave Himself as a ransom for all', 1 Timothy 2:6. The type is useful because it shows that God's justice involves substitution. It breaks down at the decisive place: in the proverb the wicked are the price, while in the gospel the innocent pays so that the wicked can go free.

study.christ:
The chapter points to Christ through three themes: the king, the sacrifice and the substitute. It never names a Messiah, so each link has to be held to what the New Testament text itself says.

The king comes first. Verse 1 is not a promise of a coming king, but it states the logic by which the New Testament reads the cross. When Jesus stands before Pilate, the Roman governor thinks he holds power. Jesus says that none would be his 'if it were not given to you from above', John 19:11. The apostles pray in Acts 4:27 to 28 and say that Herod and Pilate, with the Gentiles and Israel, did what God's hand and will had decided beforehand. The proverb explains how a plot of evil men can be a plan of God without the evil being excused.

The second theme is righteousness and justice instead of sacrifice. Jesus quotes Hosea twice to say that mercy matters more than ritual, Matthew 9:13 and 12:7, and His life is the model: He did justice and loved mercy. Yet He did not stop with condemning empty sacrifice. He became the sacrifice God provides. The Letter to the Hebrews quotes the psalm, 'Sacrifice and offering You did not desire, but a body You prepared for Me', Hebrews 10:5. The proverb shows the problem and Christ resolves it: God wants justice from His people, and He supplies in His Son the offering the unjust cannot make.

The third is the idea of substitution. Verse 18 says that the wicked become a ransom for the righteous. In the proverb's world the innocent escape because the guilty are caught. In the gospel the direction is reversed. 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf', 2 Corinthians 5:21, and the one who was righteous paid.

Verse 12's Righteous One, if read as God or the faithful king, is realised in Christ, whom Peter calls 'the Holy and Righteous One', Acts 3:14. Verse 30 and 31 find their sharpest confirmation in the empty tomb. The council planned, the soldiers sealed the stone and the horse was ready, but deliverance belongs to the LORD. Be careful of one trap: verses on quarrelsome wives, slackers and loose tongues are not secretly about Jesus. They are wisdom for ordinary life, and the gospel is better served by reading the hinge verses closely.
study.god:
The chapter's central statement about God is that He is sovereign over the one thing human beings think they hold: their own hearts, and the hearts of those who rule. Verse 1 puts the king in the LORD's hand like a ditch. Verse 2 puts every person's self-assessment under His scale. Verses 30 and 31 give a sweeping negative: no wisdom, no understanding, no counsel, and no horse prepared for battle can succeed against Him. The sentence begins with three of the great words of Proverbs, chokmah, tevunah and etsah, and says none of them has any standing against the LORD.

Yet this sovereign is never pictured as arbitrary. The God who holds the king's heart is the God who prefers righteousness and justice to sacrifice, and He is the One who weighs hearts, not merely actions. Sovereignty and moral seriousness are not in tension. The very power that turns kings is the power that cannot be bribed, which is why verse 27 says that the sacrifice of the wicked is detestable. The reasoning is that God cannot be bought by the pious show of someone who intends evil.

God is also the one who hears the cry of the poor. Verse 13 says whoever shuts his ear to that cry will cry himself and receive no answer, and it implies a God who listens first to the one the powerful ignore. Justice, in verse 15, is a joy for the righteous and terror for those who work iniquity, which means God's justice is experienced differently depending on where a person stands. It is not neutral, and it is not cruel.

There are tensions the text leaves standing. The LORD directs, and the wicked are responsible. The horse is prepared, and victory is the LORD's. The wise man can scale a fortress, verse 22, yet no wisdom prevails against the LORD, verse 30. The right way to hold them is as the sage does, by letting each statement correct the opposite temptation. Hold the first to avoid fear and the second to avoid fatalism.

For worship this means thanksgiving that no throne is outside His reach, and humility, because a true sacrifice begins with a righteous life. It also means confidence: the person who prays for rulers can do so knowing the heart they pray for is in a hand that knows what it is doing.

crossReferences.note: The LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia to send a proclamation and fulfil the word spoken through Jeremiah. A pagan monarch is moved without knowing it, which is verse 1 in historical form: the waterway turns where the LORD pleases.

After his humbling, Nebuchadnezzar confesses that God does as He pleases with the army of heaven and the peoples of the earth, and that no one can restrain His hand. The king of the greatest empire says what verse 1 had said as a general truth.

All a man's ways are pure in his own eyes, but his motives are weighed out by the LORD. This is a parallel to verse 2, using the same verb for weighing, and it shows that the idea of the LORD weighing hearts was part of the book's settled teaching.

Samuel tells Saul that obedience is better than sacrifice, and attentiveness is better than the fat of rams. It is the first narrative form of verse 3, spoken to a king who had offered worship in place of obedience.

The LORD desires mercy, not sacrifice, and knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings. Hosea brings verse 3 into the prophetic lawsuit, and Jesus later quotes the verse to defend mercy to sinners, Matthew 9:13.

The worshipper asks what to bring, thousands of rams or ten thousand rivers of oil, and is told to act justly, love mercy and walk humbly. It is the question behind verse 3 and verse 27, and the answer is the proverb's answer.

Some trust in chariots and others in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God. This is verse 31 as a song, and Israel sang what the sages taught, so that the preparation of the horse and the trust of the heart are placed on different levels.

Nations are told to devise a plan, and it will be thwarted, state a proposal and it will not happen, for God is with us. It is verse 30 spoken as an oracle during a crisis, and the closing phrase gives the reason: the LORD is on the side of His people.

Jesus tells Pilate he would have no authority unless it were given from above. Verse 1 appears here as a direct claim made by the condemned to the one who condemns, and it shows that the proverb is not a comfort for the comfortable but a truth that holds up at a cross.

Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles and Israel conspired, but did what God's hand and will had decided beforehand. This is how the early church applied the logic of verses 1 and 30: no plot could do more than God had already decided to use.

The Son of Man came to give His life as a ransom for many. It uses the same idea as verse 18's ransom but turns it around: it is not the guilty who pay for the innocent, but the innocent One who pays for the guilty.

Judgment without mercy will be shown to anyone who has not been merciful, and mercy triumphs over judgment. It is the New Testament shape of verse 13, where closing the ear to the poor leads to a cry no one answers.

study.oneStory:
Proverbs 21 is a chapter about who rules, and the Bible's story begins with that question. God gave human beings dominion in Genesis 1, and the fall was an attempt to rule without Him. By Genesis 6 the earth is full of violence. The long story of Israel is the story of what the LORD does with this: He hardens Pharaoh and then frees His people, He raises Cyrus and returns the exiles, and He raises up judges and kings and brings them down. Verse 1 is the theological summary of that history.

The question of sacrifice is also from early in the story. Cain brings an offering and is told that sin crouches at his door, so even before the law the point is that worship cannot cover wrong. In Israel the whole system of sacrifice was given as a gift for sinners and not as a way of buying off justice. The prophets are sent to those who forget this, and verse 3 is their message in advance.

Where the story is going is the cross. There the highest human power, Pilate, stands before the One who made the earth, and the highest religious establishment arranges His death. Every figure in the chapter is present: the king whose heart is in the LORD's hand, the sacrifice that is detestable when brought with ill intent, the ransom paid by the Righteous One, the counsel that cannot stand against the LORD. In the resurrection the final verse is proved. The horse was ready for the day of battle and deliverance belonged to the LORD.

The new creation is where justice, verse 15, is simply a joy. The nations bring their glory into the city, the Lamb is on the throne, and the kings of the earth, whose hearts the LORD turned all along, bring their splendour into it, Revelation 21:24. Those who loved righteousness and loving devotion, verse 21, found life, righteousness and honour, and in Christ they find them completely.

quiz.q: What does verse 1 say about the king's heart?

options.text: It is like a waterway in the LORD's hand, which He directs wherever He pleases.
options.note: Even the most powerful human will is under God's sovereign direction.

options.text: It is entirely free from any divine influence.
options.note: This is the opposite of the verse's claim.

options.text: It is only partly influenced by the LORD, mostly self-directed.
options.note: The verse's image, water directed wherever the LORD pleases, is stronger than partial influence.

options.text: It is controlled by the people's votes.
options.note: The verse names the LORD, not popular will, as the one directing the king's heart.

quiz.q: According to verse 3, what does the LORD desire more than sacrifice?

options.text: Righteousness and justice.
options.note: Ethical obedience matters more to God than ritual observance detached from it.

options.text: Wealth and prosperity.
options.note: The verse names righteousness and justice, not material prosperity.

options.text: Elaborate worship ceremonies.
options.note: This is closer to the sacrifice the verse ranks below righteousness and justice.

options.text: Personal happiness above all else.
options.note: The verse's terms are specifically righteousness and justice, not happiness in general.

quiz.q: What does verse 13 warn happens to one who shuts his ears to the poor?

options.text: He too will cry out and receive no answer.
options.note: Refusing mercy to others invites the same fate in return.

options.text: He will become wealthier as a result.
options.note: This is the opposite of the warning given.

options.text: Nothing; the verse offers no consequence.
options.note: The verse explicitly names a consequence.

options.text: He will be publicly shamed by his community.
options.note: The verse's specific consequence is being unanswered when he himself cries out, not public shaming.

quiz.q: What does verse 30 declare about human wisdom and the LORD?

options.text: No wisdom, understanding, or counsel can prevail against the LORD.
options.note: God's purposes cannot ultimately be thwarted by any human scheme.

options.text: Human wisdom is equal in power to the LORD's purposes.
options.note: This directly contradicts the verse.

options.text: Wisdom can sometimes outmaneuver the LORD's plans.
options.note: The verse's claim is absolute, not occasional.

options.text: Wisdom is unnecessary since the LORD controls everything anyway.
options.note: The chapter elsewhere commends wisdom highly, verse 22; the point of verse 30 is God's ultimate sovereignty, not that wisdom is worthless.

quiz.q: What does verse 31 say about victory in battle?

options.text: A horse is prepared for battle, but victory belongs to the LORD.
options.note: Human preparation matters, but ultimate victory is God's to give.

options.text: Victory always goes to the side with the strongest horses.
options.note: This is exactly what the verse denies.

options.text: Human preparation is pointless since the LORD decides everything.
options.note: The verse affirms preparing the horse, not dismissing preparation.

options.text: Victory is shared equally between human effort and the LORD.
options.note: The verse's structure subordinates the horse's preparation to the LORD's decisive gift of victory, not an equal partnership.

questions: Verse 1 says even a king's heart is directed by the LORD. What situation in your life, or in the news, tempts you to doubt that God is truly sovereign over it?
The LORD prizes righteousness and justice over sacrifice, verse 3. Is there a place where you substitute religious activity for actual obedience and care for others?
Verse 13 warns that shutting your ears to the poor invites the same silence back on you. Who is crying out for help nearby that you have been tuning out?
Verse 23 commends guarding the mouth and tongue to keep the soul from distress. What is one conversation this week where restraint would have served you better?
Verse 30 says no scheme can prevail against the LORD. What outcome are you anxiously trying to engineer that you need to release into God's hands instead?

translationNotes.note: 'Waterway' translates a Hebrew word for irrigation channels; the image is of a farmer directing water exactly where he wills, applied here to the LORD's total control over the king's heart.
Both verses use nearly identical language about a contentious wife, forming a matched pair within the chapter that intensifies the warning against domestic strife.

'The wicked become a ransom for the righteous' pictures divine justice using the fall of the wicked as the very means by which the righteous are spared trouble, not a doctrine of literal substitutionary payment.
